analysis.one_liner: Raises tobacco taxes roughly tenfold to fund Medicare, medical research, anti-smoking education, and aid to tobacco farmers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to raise tobacco taxes sharply, with 13 cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal excise tax on cigarettes from $12–$25.20 per thousand to $100–$210 per thousand — about a $2-per-pack increase — and raised taxes on cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco, with rates adjusted for inflation each year [S2] [S3]. It would have taxed warehouse stock and closed tax loopholes, including tax-free sales to tobacco company employees and the smuggling of tax-free "export" cigarettes back into the U.S. [S2] [S3]. Three percent of the new revenue would fund help for tobacco farmers and their communities to switch to other crops, three percent would fund public health education about tobacco risks, nine percent would go to the National Institutes of Health, and the rest would flow into Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Public health gains most: a large price increase is one of the best-documented ways to cut smoking, especially among young people. Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund would receive the bulk of the new revenue, and the National Institutes of Health would get a dedicated 9% stream for medical research. Tobacco farmers and communities hurt by the tax would get grants, loans, and transition aid from a dedicated trust fund rather than bearing the cost alone [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public health, Medicare, NIH, tobacco farmers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the cigarette tax from $12–$25.20 per thousand to $100–$210 per thousand — roughly $2 per pack — a price increase shown to reduce smoking, particularly among young smokers.
Directs the balance of the new revenue to Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, and 9% to a National Fund for Medical Research distributed to the National Institutes of Health.
Creates a Tobacco Conversion Account providing grants and loans to help farmers convert from tobacco to other crops and to help tobacco-dependent communities attract other sources of income.

Closes tax loopholes: ends tax-free sales to tobacco company employees and to the federal government, requires export-labeled tobacco to stay out of U.S. commerce, and taxes floor stocks and foreign-trade-zone inventories so companies could not stockpile pre-tax goods.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers pay the most directly — the tax is passed through in higher prices, and because smoking is more common among lower-income people, the tax falls harder on them than on the wealthy. Tobacco manufacturers and wholesalers face sharply higher taxes, a one-time tax on existing inventory, and new compliance and anti-smuggling rules. Tobacco growers would see demand fall, though the bill would dedicate part of the new revenue to compensating them [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers pay a larger share of their income than wealthier smokers, and addicted smokers who do not quit bear the full cost.
Communities dependent on tobacco growing and manufacturing would lose income even with the bill's conversion fund, which covers only 3% of new revenue and requires annual appropriations.
Large tax gaps between the U.S. and neighboring countries can create incentives for smuggling, a cost the bill tries to manage with labeling, penalties, and import restrictions rather than eliminate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a steep, lasting price increase that reduces smoking and generates revenue for Medicare and medical research, paid for mainly by smokers and the tobacco industry. The regressive burden on low-income smokers is real, and the transition aid for tobacco country is modest relative to the disruption, but the bill is deliberately structured to compensate the losers it creates rather than ignore them. As public-health tax policy, the design is more careful than most — farmers get a conversion fund, smugglers get penalties, and the revenue has dedicated destinations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1995 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Pete Stark introduced the Tobacco Health Tax and Agricultural Conversion Act of 1995 on April 6, 1995, with 11 original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over excise taxes.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
The bill attracted 13 cosponsors, 12 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the Republican majority that controlled Ways and Means in 1995 moved no tobacco tax increase.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, distributors, and growers were better off because the bill died: cigarette taxes stayed at their old low rates, and no revenue flowed to Medicare, NIH, or tobacco-farmer transition aid. Smokers kept paying pre-1995 prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and smokers paying old prices

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and senior Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and used his seat on the tax-writing committee to propose a large tobacco tax increase with dedicated spending.

for.name: 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.role: House cosponsors including Dick Durbin, Nancy Pelosi, James Hansen (R-UT), and Cardiss Collins
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors across party lines, including the bill's only Republican, James Hansen of Utah.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and majority of the committee with jurisdiction over excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — allowing it to expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers and leaf-growing interests
against.what_they_did: The tobacco industry was a well-known, active opponent of federal tobacco tax increases during this period; no industry action on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 12 Democrats and 1 Republican backed the bill — but no vote was ever taken, so party positions on the merits were never recorded; the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have raised excise taxes on their products roughly tenfold, taxed existing warehouse inventory, ended tax-free employee and government sales, and tightened anti-smuggling rules against re-importing tax-free export cigarettes. Manufacturers' interest in defeating it ran against the public-health and Medicare purposes of the tax.

A tenfold tax increase would cut demand for their leaf, but the bill dedicates 3% of new revenue to grants, loans, and conversion assistance to move farmers to other crops and diversify their communities — compensation other industries facing a tax do not get.
Retailers would owe a one-time floor-stocks tax on inventory held when the new rates took effect, with only a $500 credit and limited vending-machine relief, and higher prices would cut sales volume.
The bill imposes a new $29.34-per-pound excise tax on roll-your-own tobacco, which had previously escaped the cigarette tax, closing a price advantage over manufactured cigarettes.
